cultivar: Jin Guan Yin (Tieguanyin × Huang Dan hybrid, Mingke No. 1 / 204)
processing: In Wuyi: medium-light oxidation, strip-rolled and lightly to medium charcoal roasted to keep its aroma. In Anxi the same cultivar is also ball-rolled in the green Tieguanyin style.
harvest_season: Spring, picked earlier than the old Wuyi cultivars, usually mid to late April, as mature shoots with three or four open leaves.
appearance_dry: Tight, slightly thin dark olive strips with a strong sweet-floral smell from the bag.
appearance_wet: Medium-sized, soft, yellow-green leaves with reddish rims, close to Tieguanyin in shape.
taste_profile: A Tieguanyin-like orchid aroma over honey and light toast, sweet and easy, with a lighter body and a shorter mineral finish than yancha from the old bushes.

brewing.notes: Boiling water in a porcelain gaiwan. Keep steeps short: the aroma is the point and it is gone if you stew the leaf. Expect six or seven good infusions.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year; being an early sprouter it is picked, roasted and often on sale ahead of the classic Wuyi cultivars, usually by late summer, with the year stated. Its light roast means it is best within a year or two and it is not an ageing tea.
description:
Jin Guan Yin is a modern, institute-bred cultivar that gives Wuyi makers a cheap, strongly aromatic rock tea, and gives drinkers a half-way house between Anxi Tieguanyin and yancha: the orchid perfume of the first with the strip leaf and roast of the second.

It was bred at the Fujian Tea Research Institute by crossing Tieguanyin (as mother) with Huang Dan, the cultivar behind Huang Jin Gui, in work running from 1978 to 1999, and is known as Mingke No. 1, trade number 204; one trade list dates its release to 2000. It sprouts early, yields well and carries aroma easily, so it was planted widely across Fujian; its sibling from the same cross is Huang Guan Yin.

In Wuyi it is picked in mid to late April, before the old cultivars, oxidised to a medium-light level and given a light to medium charcoal roast. Heavier roasting kills the orchid note, so makers rarely push it. In Anxi and elsewhere in southern Fujian the same leaf is ball-rolled and sold green-style, and it also turns up as a black tea; the Wuyi strip-roasted version is the one most people meet.

The first two steeps are all flowers and honey, close to a lightly roasted Tieguanyin; the middle steeps add toast and a gentle sweetness, and by the sixth it fades. Body and aftertaste are lighter than a Shui Xian or a Rou Gui, which is the trade-off for the fragrance and the price. Brew hot, with a gaiwan and quick pours.

It is sold by the current spring harvest and should be drunk within a year or two. It is often used in Da Hong Pao blends to lift the aroma, and a lot of very cheap aromatic Da Hong Pao is mostly Jin Guan Yin and Huang Guan Yin; nothing wrong with that as long as the price reflects it. If you like it, try Huang Guan Yin next and compare the two siblings.
sources_note: Parentage (Tieguanyin × Huang Dan), the Mingke No. 1 name, number 204 and the 2002 national registration are from Chinese cultivar lists; worth a fact-check against the Huang Guan Yin entry (Mingke No. 2 / 105), as the two are often mixed up.
history:
Jin Guan Yin is a bred cultivar with a clear record. It was developed between 1978 and 1999 by crossing Tieguanyin as mother with Huang Jin Gui as father, and it is also known as Mingke No. 1. In the Wuyi area it goes by the number 204, and a trade list of Fujian Tea Research Institute varieties dates it to 2000.

From there it became a widely used aromatic clone. It is made in Wuyi as a strip-rolled roasted tea, and also as a lighter, fragrant oolong.
